name: Local Network Access (local-network)
plain: Asks to let a public site talk to devices on your home or office network.
meaning: Blocks a public website from reaching private IP addresses (printers, routers, smart devices) unless you allow it. Closes the old way for sites to scan or attack your LAN from the browser.

access.prompt_ui: Chrome prompt: Look for and connect to any device on your local network, Allow or Block. Applies to subresource requests from public sites to private IPs.
steps: Page requests a private address (RFC 1918, link local, .local)
Chrome checks address space of site vs target

firefox.note: staged rollout of Local Network Access from 147 (ETP Strict 149, all users 151, default 153)

limits.headline: Can find and connect to devices on your home or office network, if you tap Allow
limits.user_action: You visit a site that needs your printer, router or smart device and tap Allow
can: Look for and connect to devices on your local network once you allow it
Set up or control smart home gear and printers from a web page
Keep that access until you change it in site settings
cannot: Reach local devices before you allow it in Chrome and Edge
Work in Safari or on iPhone browsers
Scan your network silently, which the pop up was added to stop
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge ask with a pop up. Firefox is partial. Safari, iPhone browsers and Samsung Internet do not offer it.

story.what_it_is: Your browser asks if a website may talk to devices on your home or office network.

marketing.name: Local Network Access
marketing.pitch: Chrome asks first when a public site wants to reach devices on your local network, to prevent hidden attacks on home gear.

story.for_you: A prompt asks if the site may look for and connect to devices on your network. Allow it only for sites you trust and need it for, like a printer setup page. Choosing block keeps your devices hidden.
story.for_makers: Makers of devices with web setup pages and cloud dashboards must ask. It is a clear moment to explain why access is needed. Sites that scan without a reason get blocked and lose trust.

use_cases.example: A thermostat's website asks to find the device on your Wi-Fi, so setup finishes in the browser with no app.
A web remote for a speaker asks to find speakers at home, then plays your playlist on them.
A web streaming page for a home gaming PC asks to find the PC on your network, and then starts a low delay stream.
A company's cloud print portal finds a printer on the office network after one allow.
A browser based dev tool reaches a test device on the lab network for debugging.
A shady page tries to reach your router's admin page. The browser prompt warns you and you can say no.
A web casting page looks for TVs on your Wi-Fi so you can send a video to the big screen.

technical_bounds: Applies to secure and mixed contexts
Does not cover navigations, only subresources
Later split into local-network and loopback-network

abuse: LAN scanning and router attacks from a webpage

history.change: Firefox begins tests of Local Network Access
